query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of carbon (e.g., 0.3 at%) into a MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy will form stable carbide precipitates that enhance high-temperature strength by at least 10% relative to the undoped baseline, without significantly raising density or degrading room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy with homogeneous microstructure and grain size near 50 µm.
generation.intervention: Add ~0.3 at% carbon to the alloy melt prior to solidification.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at both room temperature (20°C) and elevated temperature (≥1200°C) under standard vacuum (~10^-5 Torr) and a strain rate of ~10^-3 s^-1.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale carbide precipitates that impede dislocation motion and stabilize grain boundaries at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The fine carbide dispersions serve as obstacles to slip and grain-boundary sliding, preserving strength at elevated temperatures without significantly altering baseline density.
generation.predicted_outcome: A ≥10% increase in 0.2% yield strength at ~1200°C compared to the undoped alloy, with comparable or better room-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The same MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy without carbon additions.
generation.boundary: If the carbides dissolve or coarsen excessively above 1100°C, or if the carbon addition embrittles the alloy at ambient conditions, this hypothesis may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: Extent of strength improvement could vary by ±5% depending on processing route and grain size; room-temperature fracture toughness changes remain less precisely defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy batches: one with ~0.3 at% C, one baseline without C. Subject both to room-temperature and 1200°C compression or tensile tests in vacuum under identical strain rates, and compare microstructures by TEM/EDS before and after testing.
measurements: Tensile ductility and fracture toughness at 20°C
TEM/EDS to identify and quantify carbide precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Failure to achieve at least a 10% strength improvement at 1200°C or observing a significant drop (>5% absolute) in room-temperature ductility invalidates the hypothesis.
